details:
**Catch-22 paradox and Doc Daneeka**
The title rule, explained to Yossarian by the flight surgeon Doc Daneeka: a pilot who is crazy can be grounded, but he has to ask, and anyone who asks to stop flying combat missions is showing a rational concern for his own safety and so is sane. Yossarian lets out a "respectful whistle" at its "absolute simplicity," and later the catch is described as a law that nobody is allowed to read. The phrase has entered English as a name for any no-win situation built on circular logic.

**Milo Minderbinder and M&M Enterprises**
Milo is the squadron's mess officer, who turns his job into a huge black-market syndicate called M&M Enterprises. He adds an ampersand and a second "M" to make his one-man company look like a partnership, and he insists that "everybody has a share." He later becomes the Vice-Shah of Oran, Imam of Damascus, and Caliph of Baghdad, and he is court-martialed after he takes a German contract to bomb his own squadron's base on Pianosa.

**Eggs bought for seven cents and sold for five**
Milo's most famous scheme. He buys eggs in Malta for seven cents each and sells them to the mess halls for five cents each, yet still makes a profit through a circular series of sales between his own syndicate and the military.

**Chocolate-covered Egyptian cotton**
After M&M Enterprises buys up the world's entire supply of Egyptian cotton and cannot sell it, Milo dips the cotton in chocolate and tries to serve it to the men in the mess hall as candy (a joke on "cotton candy").

**Major Major Major Major**
An officer whose father named him Major Major Major as a joke, and whom an IBM machine "with a sense of humor" then promotes to the rank of major. He is said to look like Henry Fonda. A shy man, he jumps out of his office window to avoid talking to people and only sees visitors when he is not there. He is beaten up while wearing a disguise during a basketball game.

**Snowden ("I'm cold")**
A young gunner hit by flak during a mission over Avignon. Yossarian treats an obvious wound in his thigh, then finds that his guts are spilling out under his flak suit, and Snowden keeps saying "I'm cold" while Yossarian answers "There, there." From this Yossarian concludes that "the spirit gone, man is garbage." He also asks, "Where are the Snowdens of yesteryear?" (a play on Villon's "Where are the snows of yesteryear?").

**Yossarian naked in a tree**
After Snowden's death, Yossarian refuses to wear clothes because Snowden's blood had soaked his uniform. He sits naked in a tree during Snowden's funeral and later receives a medal while naked in formation.

**"Washington Irving" and the chaplain**
While in the hospital, Yossarian censors enlisted men's letters at random and signs some of them "Washington Irving" (or "Irving Washington"). C.I.D. (Criminal Investigation Division) men come to investigate, and the suspicion falls on Chaplain Tappman, an Anabaptist, who is then interrogated. The novel's opening line, "It was love at first sight," describes Yossarian's first meeting with the chaplain, and Yossarian is in the hospital with a "pain in his liver that fell just short of being jaundice."

**Nately's whore**
The Roman prostitute who is loved by the young, idealistic pilot Nately. When Nately is killed, she blames Yossarian and keeps trying to kill him. In the chapter titled "Catch-22," she stabs him with a bone-handled kitchen knife just after he accepts Colonels Cathcart and Korn's deal.

**Colonel Cathcart and the rising mission count**
The group commander, who keeps raising the number of missions his men must fly before they can be sent home, hoping it will get him promoted to general and get his picture in The Saturday Evening Post. Near the end he and Colonel Korn offer Yossarian an "odious" deal: he can go home if he agrees to praise them.

**Orr and the escape to Sweden**
Yossarian's tent-mate, a tinkerer who stuffs crab apples or horse chestnuts in his cheeks and says crab apples are better because of their shape. He keeps crash-landing his plane in the sea, which turns out to be practice. At the end of the novel Yossarian learns that Orr has rowed to neutral Sweden, and Yossarian deserts to follow him.

**Kid Sampson and McWatt**
McWatt, a cheerful pilot who likes to buzz the beach with his plane, flies too low and his propeller cuts Kid Sampson in half. Overcome with guilt, McWatt then flies his plane into a mountain and kills himself.

**Doc Daneeka declared dead**
Doc Daneeka has his name put on McWatt's flight log to collect flight pay without flying, so he is officially listed as dead when McWatt crashes. His wife receives a form letter about the death of "your husband, son, father or brother," collects the insurance and pension money, and moves to Lansing, Michigan, while the living doctor is ignored by everyone.

**Pianosa and the Great Big Siege of Bologna**
The novel is set at an American bomber base on the small Mediterranean island of Pianosa, off Italy. Before a feared raid on Bologna, Yossarian secretly moves the string on the map that marks the front line so that the city seems to have been captured, which gets the mission called off for a while.

**Hungry Joe and Chief White Halfoat**
Hungry Joe is a pilot who claims to have been a Life magazine photographer and keeps trying to photograph naked women; he has screaming nightmares whenever he is not flying missions. Chief White Halfoat, a Native American who shares a tent with Doc Daneeka, says his family was a "human divining rod" because oil companies kept finding oil wherever they settled and forcing them to move, and he predicts he will die of pneumonia.
